title: Ovarian Torsion: Sudden Unilateral Pelvic Pain With Nausea Needs Urgent Evaluation
bottomLine: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic or lower-abdominal pain, often with nausea/vomiting, can indicate adnexal torsion. Timely surgical evaluation matters because preserved Doppler flow does not reliably exclude intermittent or partial torsion.
recognize: Pain may be intermittent; ovarian cyst/mass history can increase risk.
priorities: Assess hemodynamic stability and pain, keep NPO as ordered, and escalate promptly for gynecologic evaluation.
assessMonitor: Pain onset/location, nausea/vomiting, abdominal findings, vital signs, pregnancy status/testing as ordered, and imaging results.
interventions: Provide ordered analgesia/antiemetics and prepare for urgent diagnostic/surgical management.
medicationSafety: Analgesia should not be withheld solely to preserve examination findings; medication does not correct torsion.
teaching: Sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain with vomiting requires urgent care.
delegationScope: Routine vitals may be delegated; acute pelvic-pain interpretation and escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Ruling out torsion because Doppler flow is still present.
oneLinePearl: Torsion is a time-sensitive surgical diagnosis; normal flow does not always exclude it.

title: Acute Abnormal Uterine Bleeding: Hemodynamic Stability Comes First
bottomLine: Heavy uterine bleeding can cause acute blood loss even without pregnancy. Assess hemodynamic stability first, quantify bleeding trends, and escalate syncope, tachycardia, hypotension, severe weakness, or ongoing heavy loss.
recognize: Frequent pad/tampon saturation, large clots, dizziness, pallor, and exertional dyspnea suggest clinically important blood loss.
priorities: Assess ABCs/perfusion, pregnancy status as ordered, bleeding severity, and obtain urgent gynecologic evaluation when unstable or ongoing.
assessMonitor: BP/HR, orthostatic symptoms, bleeding amount, mental status, CBC/type-and-screen/coagulation studies as ordered.
interventions: Maintain IV access and prepare for fluids, blood products, hormonal or procedural treatment according to orders.
medicationSafety: Hormonal and antifibrinolytic choices depend on contraindications and bleeding risk; do not independently select therapy.
teaching: Seek urgent care for heavy bleeding with fainting, severe weakness, chest symptoms, or shortness of breath.
delegationScope: Pad counts/vitals may be delegated; hemodynamic interpretation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Focusing on cycle irregularity while missing shock signs.
oneLinePearl: In acute uterine bleeding, stabilize first and diagnose the cause second.
sourceBasis: ACOG acute abnormal uterine bleeding guidance

title: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease: Pelvic Pain Plus Fever or Cervical Findings Needs Prompt Treatment
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Lower abdominal or pelvic pain with fever, abnormal discharge, dyspareunia, cervical motion/adnexal tenderness, or STI risk can indicate PID. Prompt evaluation and treatment reduce infertility and abscess risk.
recognize: Symptoms can be mild; pregnancy, appendicitis, torsion, and ectopic pregnancy remain important alternatives.
priorities: Assess pain, fever, pregnancy possibility, sepsis cues, and ability to tolerate oral therapy; notify the provider promptly.
assessMonitor: Vitals, pelvic/abdominal symptoms, discharge, vomiting, medication adherence, and response to prescribed antibiotics.
interventions: Administer ordered antimicrobials, reinforce partner/STI management and follow-up, and escalate worsening symptoms.
medicationSafety: Complete the full prescribed regimen; avoid alcohol or interacting medications when relevant to the selected antibiotics.
teaching: Avoid sex until treatment/follow-up criteria are met and partners are managed according to the plan.
delegationScope: Teaching reinforcement is appropriate; diagnosis/regimen selection is provider-led.
examTrap: Waiting for severe fever before taking pelvic pain and discharge seriously.
oneLinePearl: PID can be subtle, but delayed treatment has long-term reproductive consequences.

title: Tubo-Ovarian Abscess: Fever, Pelvic Mass, or Toxic Appearance Needs Escalation
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: PID complicated by persistent fever, severe unilateral/bilateral pelvic pain, adnexal mass, vomiting, or systemic illness may indicate tubo-ovarian abscess. Escalate because rupture can cause sepsis and peritonitis.
recognize: Failure to improve on outpatient PID therapy is an important cue.
priorities: Assess sepsis/peritoneal signs and notify gynecology promptly.
assessMonitor: Vitals, pain, abdominal guarding, vomiting, WBC/inflammatory labs and imaging results as ordered.
interventions: Support ordered IV antibiotics, fluids, pain control, and drainage/surgical planning.
medicationSafety: Broad-spectrum antibiotic selection and duration are provider directed.
teaching: Return urgently for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, or faintness.
delegationScope: Routine monitoring may be delegated; sepsis/peritonitis interpretation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Continuing routine outpatient teaching despite worsening fever and focal pelvic pain.
oneLinePearl: PID that worsens despite treatment needs abscess evaluation.

title: After Hysterectomy: Heavy Bleeding or Shock Is Not Expected Recovery
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After hysterectomy, small expected drainage depends on procedure, but heavy vaginal bleeding, increasing abdominal distention, tachycardia, hypotension, severe pain, or syncope can indicate hemorrhage and needs urgent surgical review.
recognize: Internal bleeding may exceed visible vaginal loss.
priorities: Assess hemodynamics, abdomen/incisions, vaginal loss, urine output, and escalate promptly.
assessMonitor: BP/HR, pain, abdominal girth/distention, dressing/drain output, vaginal bleeding, urine output, and ordered CBC.
interventions: Maintain IV access, NPO status as ordered, and prepare for hemorrhage management.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants and NSAIDs may affect bleeding risk; do not independently stop prescribed therapy without urgent review.
teaching: After discharge, report heavy bleeding, fever, severe pain, or faintness promptly.
delegationScope: Routine output/vitals may be delegated; deterioration interpretation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Calling worsening tachycardia normal postoperative anxiety despite increasing abdominal distention.
oneLinePearl: Post-hysterectomy shock can be internal bleeding even with little vaginal blood.
sourceBasis: Contemporary U.S. postoperative gynecologic care principles

title: Vaginal Cuff Dehiscence: Sudden Pelvic Pressure, Bleeding, or Tissue at the Vagina Is an Emergency
bottomLine: After hysterectomy, sudden pelvic pain/pressure, bleeding, watery discharge, or protruding tissue can indicate vaginal cuff dehiscence or evisceration. Protect exposed tissue and obtain immediate surgical care.
recognize: Symptoms may follow intercourse, straining, infection, or occur spontaneously.
priorities: Call surgical emergency help, keep the patient supine, avoid vaginal manipulation, and protect exposed tissue with sterile moist dressing if present per protocol.
assessMonitor: Hemodynamics, pain, bleeding, visible tissue, abdominal findings, and infection signs.
interventions: Maintain NPO/IV support and prepare for operative repair.
medicationSafety: Analgesics/antibiotics are ordered adjuncts and do not replace urgent repair.
teaching: Follow postoperative pelvic/activity restrictions and report sudden pressure, bleeding, or tissue protrusion.
delegationScope: Emergency support is immediate; vaginal examination/repair is provider-led.
examTrap: Attempting to push protruding tissue back into the vagina.
oneLinePearl: Post-hysterectomy tissue protrusion is a surgical emergency—cover, protect, escalate.
sourceBasis: Contemporary U.S. gynecologic postoperative emergency principles

title: After Cervical Procedure: Heavy Bleeding or Fever Requires Reassessment
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After cervical biopsy, LEEP, or conization, mild expected discharge varies, but heavy bleeding, foul discharge, fever, severe pelvic pain, or syncope can indicate hemorrhage or infection.
recognize: Patients may confuse normal dark discharge from hemostatic agents with bleeding; amount and symptoms matter.
priorities: Assess bleeding severity, hemodynamics, fever/pain, and contact the procedural team for concerning findings.
assessMonitor: Pad counts, BP/HR, temperature, discharge odor, pelvic pain, and dizziness.
interventions: Reinforce procedure-specific pelvic/activity restrictions and arrange urgent evaluation when needed.
medicationSafety: Verify instructions before aspirin/NSAID use when bleeding risk is relevant.
teaching: Know which discharge is expected and which bleeding/fever symptoms require urgent contact.
delegationScope: Routine teaching may be reinforced; postprocedure complication interpretation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Calling any dark discharge hemorrhage without assessing amount and associated symptoms.
oneLinePearl: After cervical procedures, symptoms plus bleeding volume determine urgency.

title: Sexual Assault Care: Safety, Consent, Evidence Options, and Trauma-Informed Support
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Sexual-assault care prioritizes immediate medical safety, patient consent, trauma-informed communication, forensic options, STI/pregnancy prevention options, and jurisdiction-specific reporting requirements. Do not pressure the patient into police reporting or evidence collection when the law allows choice.
recognize: Strangulation, head injury, severe bleeding, pregnancy risk, intoxication, and suicidal distress require additional urgent assessment.
priorities: Ensure privacy/safety, treat urgent injuries, preserve choices, and activate trained sexual-assault resources.
assessMonitor: Injuries, strangulation symptoms, pain, pregnancy/STI risk, mental-health safety, and support needs.
interventions: Offer forensic examination, advocacy, prophylaxis, emergency contraception, and follow-up according to consent, age, law, and protocol.
medicationSafety: STI prophylaxis and emergency contraception are regimen-specific and provider/protocol directed.
teaching: Explain options without coercion and provide written follow-up resources when safe.
delegationScope: Forensic examination and reporting requirements depend on training, role, age, jurisdiction, and facility policy.
examTrap: Collecting evidence or contacting police without explaining consent/reporting rules.
oneLinePearl: Trauma-informed care preserves safety and patient choice wherever the law permits.

title: Bartholin Abscess: Severe Vulvar Pain and Swelling May Need Drainage
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: A painful fluctuant vulvar mass can indicate Bartholin gland abscess. Assess fever/systemic illness and escalate for drainage/gynecologic treatment rather than repeatedly treating pain alone.
recognize: Walking, sitting, or intercourse may become very painful; fever can occur.
priorities: Assess pain, size/location, fever, drainage, pregnancy/immunocompromise context, and arrange provider evaluation.
assessMonitor: Temperature, pain, swelling, spontaneous drainage, and recurrence.
interventions: Provide ordered analgesia, sitz-bath comfort measures when appropriate, and prepare for drainage procedure.
medicationSafety: Antibiotics are not automatically required for every cyst/abscess; indication depends on clinical context and procedure plan.
teaching: Avoid squeezing or self-lancing and return for worsening fever/pain.
delegationScope: Comfort care may be reinforced; incision/drainage requires qualified provider.
examTrap: Assuming every painful vulvar mass should be treated only with antibiotics.
oneLinePearl: A painful fluctuant Bartholin abscess is often a drainage problem, not just a medication problem.

title: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding in Adolescents: Screen for Anemia and Bleeding Disorders
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Heavy menstrual bleeding in adolescents can be the first sign of a bleeding disorder. Assess hemodynamic stability and anemia symptoms, and support evaluation for bleeding history rather than assuming all early cycles are normal.
recognize: Flooding, frequent product changes, prolonged menses, easy bruising, epistaxis, family bleeding history, or prior excessive surgical/dental bleeding raise concern.
priorities: Assess stability, fatigue/dizziness, bleeding severity, and notify the clinician for CBC/iron and bleeding-disorder evaluation as indicated.
assessMonitor: BP/HR, orthostatic symptoms, bleeding pattern, hemoglobin/ferritin/coagulation testing as ordered.
interventions: Reinforce prescribed iron/hormonal or other treatment and follow-up.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs, hormonal therapy, and antifibrinolytics have context-specific benefits/risks; do not generalize treatment without evaluation.
redFlags: Chest symptoms or dyspnea from anemia
teaching: Tracking bleeding amount/duration can help identify abnormal patterns and treatment response.
delegationScope: History reinforcement and vitals may be shared; treatment selection is provider-led.
examTrap: Telling an adolescent that very heavy bleeding is normal because menarche was recent.
oneLinePearl: Heavy adolescent menses can reveal a bleeding disorder—ask about the whole bleeding history.
